title: What is a municipal bond?
subtitle: Local-government bonds that fund public infrastructure
openingQuestion: A city government wants to build a new bridge but has a limited budget. What financing tool fits?
openingOptions: Take an ordinary commercial bank loan
There's no option besides asking the central budget for money
Issue a municipal bond to raise capital from investors, repaid from taxes or fees generated by the project
explanation: A municipal bond (muni) is a bond issued by a local government or public authority to fund infrastructure: schools, roads and bridges, public hospitals. The repayment source is usually local taxes (general obligation) or the specific project's revenue (revenue bond).

diagram.label: A locality needs capital to build schools, bridges, hospitals
Debt is repaid from local taxes or the project's own revenue
Usually comes with a tax benefit, making it attractive to individual investors

realWorldExample.description: The US municipal bond market is worth trillions of dollars, popular because the interest earned is usually exempt from federal income tax - attractive to high-income individual investors.

quiz.question: How does a revenue bond differ from a general obligation bond?
options: A revenue bond is backed by the entire local government budget
A revenue bond relies only on the cash flow of that specific project
A revenue bond always has a shorter maturity than a GO bond
A revenue bond is tax-exempt while a GO bond is fully taxable
quiz.explanation: A GO bond is backed by the 'full faith and credit' of the government - using its taxing power to repay debt. A revenue bond depends only on cash flow from the specific project (say, toll fees on a bridge), so it carries higher risk if the project doesn't generate enough revenue.

quiz.question: Why do US municipal bonds typically yield noticeably less than corporate bonds with the same credit rating?
options: Because municipal bonds are far more liquid
Because local governments almost never default
Because the interest earned is usually exempt from federal income tax
Because municipal bonds typically have much shorter maturities
quiz.explanation: The tax benefit is the decisive factor that makes municipal bonds attractive despite a lower stated rate - high-income investors (facing a high tax bracket) often find a muni's AFTER-TAX yield far more competitive than a fully taxable corporate bond.

quiz.question: An investor in the 35% tax bracket is choosing between a tax-exempt 3.5% muni and a taxable 5% corporate bond. Which is better?
options: Cannot compare without knowing the credit rating first
The corporate bond, because 5% is higher than 3.5%
The two are equal once every kind of tax is accounted for
The muni, because 5% after tax leaves only 3.25%
quiz.explanation: The muni's tax-equivalent yield = 3.5% / (1 − 0.35) = 5.4%, higher than 5%. This is why munis are most attractive to investors in a high tax bracket, and nearly pointless for those in a low one.

quiz.question: Why does a revenue bond typically yield more than a general obligation bond from the same locality?
options: Because its repayment source is narrower, so its risk is higher
Because revenue bonds receive no tax benefit at all
Because revenue bonds always have longer maturities
Because a GO bond is guaranteed by the federal government
quiz.explanation: A GO bond rests on the taxing power of the whole locality; a revenue bond rests on one specific project - if a toll bridge sees fewer cars than expected, there's no other source to fall back on.

quiz.question: What is the most notable difference between local-government bonds in Vietnam and in the US?
options: Only cities directly under central management are allowed to issue them
The market is still very small and lacks a similar tax benefit
Their yield is always higher than corporate bonds
Individual investors are banned from buying local-government bonds
quiz.explanation: A muni's appeal in the US comes almost entirely from the federal tax benefit. Without that mechanism, local-government bonds have to compete on plain yield alone, which is why the market stays quite small.

keyTakeaways: Municipal bond: funds public infrastructure at the local-government level
Two main types: General Obligation (backed by general taxes) and Revenue bond (backed by project revenue)
Usually comes with a tax benefit, attractive to individual investors

practicePrompt.question: A city government issues bonds to fund roads, bridges, and public schools, paying interest from local tax revenue. What is this kind of bond called, and how does it differ from a central government's treasury bond?
options: This is a treasury bond, since any bond issued by a government body is generally called a treasury bond
Municipal bond: issued by a local government to fund public projects
This is a corporate bond, since the city government is acting like a company by issuing bonds
There is no meaningful difference between a municipal bond and a treasury bond in nature or risk
practicePrompt.explanation: Municipal bond: funds public infrastructure at the local-government level. Unlike a treasury bond (issued by the central government), a municipal bond is issued by a local government to fund specific public projects, and its risk depends on that locality's own financial condition.

summary.keyIdea: Municipal bond: funds public infrastructure at the local-government level
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Two main types: General Obligation (backed by general taxes) and Revenue bond (backed by project revenue)

application.title: Find a real municipal bond
application.message: The lesson already explained why municipal bonds are barely developed in Vietnam - reread the section above before searching, so you don't spend time hunting for something that doesn't commonly exist yet.
application.secondary: Not finding one is fine - the search itself sharpens your grasp of general obligation and revenue bonds.

sections.text: When a city in the US needs to build a new school or repair a bridge, it usually does more than just draw on its existing tax budget - it issues a municipal bond (muni) to raise long-term capital from investors.
Two types of municipal bond: General Obligation and Revenue

A General Obligation bond (GO bond) is backed by the 'full faith and credit' of the local government - its repayment source is the general tax budget, so its risk is relatively low as long as that locality's fiscal health is sound. A revenue bond is different: its repayment source comes only from the cash flow of the specific funded project - say, fees collected from a toll bridge, or revenue from a public hospital. If the project doesn't generate the revenue expected, a revenue bond carries noticeably more risk than a GO bond, even though both are 'local government' bonds.
The tax benefit: why muni bonds appeal despite a lower rate

The special feature that attracts high-income US investors to municipal bonds is that the interest earned is usually exempt from federal income tax (and sometimes state tax too, if buying a bond from one's own state of residence). Because of this tax benefit, investors accept a stated rate noticeably lower than a corporate bond with the same credit rating - but a muni's actual AFTER-TAX yield can be equal to or even higher. This is why the US municipal bond market is worth trillions of dollars, held largely by individual investors facing a high tax rate.

items: GO bond: repaid from the locality's general tax budget
Revenue bond: repaid from the funded project's own revenue - higher risk than a GO bond
The federal income-tax exemption is the main reason investors accept a lower stated rate
Always compare AFTER-TAX yield when weighing a muni bond against other bond types

sections.text: The reality in Vietnam: municipal bonds barely exist

items: Unlike the US (where municipal bonds form a large market with a tax benefit), Vietnam has no comparably developed local-government bond market

A handful of localities (like Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi) have issued small-scale urban/project bonds to fund infrastructure, but this is uncommon and there is no liquid secondary market like there is for government bonds
Most local infrastructure in Vietnam is funded through the state budget, ODA, or centrally issued government bonds - not through a dedicated municipal bond channel

sections.label: Why you'll struggle to find an example
sections.text: This is an accurate observation about the market, not a search error on your part: a municipal bond in the full sense (issued by a local government, repaid from a local budget/tax source, traded regularly in a secondary market) barely exists in Vietnam at this point.
